name: Slobodan Kačar

early_history_summary: Born in Jajce, Bosnia to a farming family that moved to Novi Sad when he was a teenager. Inspired by Muhammad Ali and Yugoslav boxer Mate Parlov, Kačar and his older brother Tadija started boxing at a club in Novi Sad. He compiled a reported amateur record of 241-9, winning bronze at the 1978 World Championships and gold at the 1979 Mediterranean Games before his Olympic triumph in 1980.
family_context_summary: Born to a farming family in rural Bosnia; parents worked abroad in Germany while children were raised by grandparents. Family moved to Novi Sad, Serbia in the early 1970s. His older brother Tadija was also a boxer who won Olympic silver in 1976.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family boxing background documented; however, his older brother Tadija Kačar was an accomplished boxer (Olympic silver 1976) who trained at the same club, creating a sibling-driven training environment.

evidence_summary: Kačar grew up in a rural Bosnian family with modest means; his parents worked abroad while he was raised by grandparents. He and his older brother Tadija, an Olympic silver medalist boxer, started boxing together at a club in Novi Sad. The Yugoslav amateur boxing system provided a strong competitive pipeline. Kačar compiled an exceptional amateur record of 241-9, winning World Championship bronze at 20 and Olympic gold at 22. The sibling boxing partnership and the Yugoslav boxing ecosystem were key early advantages.

name: Tim Duncan
milestone_by_age_26: Won NBA championship and NBA Finals MVP with the San Antonio Spurs in 1999 at age 23, after being drafted #1 overall in 1997 and winning NBA Rookie of the Year in 1998.
early_history_summary: Born on Saint Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands, Duncan initially aspired to be an Olympic swimmer. After Hurricane Hugo destroyed the island's pool in 1989 and his mother died of cancer in 1990, he switched to basketball at age 14, taught by his brother-in-law. He played at St. Dunstan's Episcopal High School and then Wake Forest University (1993-97), where he became a consensus All-American and National College Player of the Year. Drafted #1 overall by the San Antonio Spurs in 1997, he won Rookie of the Year in 1998 and the NBA championship with Finals MVP in 1999.
family_context_summary: Born to Ione (a midwife) and William Duncan (a mason) on Saint Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands. Both parents were immigrants from Anguilla. His mother died of breast cancer in 1990 when Duncan was 14. His sister Tricia swam for the U.S. Virgin Islands at the 1988 Olympics.
parent_family_domain_summary: No basketball background in family; sister was an Olympic swimmer and brother-in-law Ricky Lowery was a former Division III basketball player who taught Duncan the game. Family valued education, with mother's deathbed wish that Duncan graduate from college.

evidence_summary: Duncan grew up in the U.S. Virgin Islands in a working-class immigrant family. He started basketball late at 14 after his mother's death and a hurricane destroyed swimming facilities. His brother-in-law, a former college player, provided initial coaching. Wake Forest University's coaching staff discovered him and developed him into a national college player of the year. The San Antonio Spurs drafted him #1 overall in 1997, and he won Rookie of the Year and then NBA championship with Finals MVP by age 23. His late start was offset by exceptional physical attributes and the elite NBA pipeline of the Spurs organization alongside David Robinson.

name: Alena Vrzáňová
milestone_by_age_26: Won the World Figure Skating Championships in Paris in 1949 at age 17, becoming the first Czechoslovakian world champion in ladies' singles; also won a second world title in 1950 at age 19.
early_history_summary: Born in Prague in 1931 to a musical family (father a professional cellist, mother an opera singer), Vrzáňová began skating at a young age during WWII, training in difficult conditions at the open Štvanice Stadium. She won the Czechoslovak junior national championship in 1946 at age 15. In early 1947, she moved to Richmond, London to train under renowned coach Arnold Gerschwiler. She won the Czechoslovak national championship from 1947 to 1950, placed 7th at the 1947 Worlds, 5th at the 1948 Olympics, and won her first World title in 1949 at age 17, credited as the first woman to land a double Lutz jump in competition.
family_context_summary: Born into a musical family in Prague; father was a professional cello player who worked in the Ministry of Finance, mother was an opera singer. Parents encouraged her skating and later supported her defection from Czechoslovakia.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family skating background; however, the family's musical background (father cellist, mother opera singer) provided an artistic foundation. Father worked in the Ministry of Finance, suggesting a middle-class professional family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Arnold Gerschwiler coaching, Richmond Ice Rink, musical family, wartime training, double Lutz, defection
evidence_summary: Vrzáňová was born into a musical, middle-class family in Prague and began skating during WWII under difficult conditions. At 15, she won the Czechoslovak junior national championship. The pivotal moment was moving to London in 1947 at age 16 to train under Arnold Gerschwiler, a renowned Swiss coach at the Richmond Ice Rink. Under Gerschwiler's sustained coaching, she transformed into the world's best skater, winning World titles in 1949 and 1950. She was the first woman to land a double Lutz in competition. Her father, a Ministry of Finance employee, supported her training abroad and later encouraged her defection.

current_position: Died on July 30, 2015 at age 84 in New York City; final role: retired professional figure skater who performed with Ice Follies and Ice Capades for 16 years, later restaurant owner and public relations manager for Ice Capades in New York.
